text: One of the big tests in this election was running Bernie Sanders style Democrats in places that
are purple or even in sort of plus Trump territory. There were a bunch of really interesting candidates
who showed us what that can look like. Candidates like Sam Forstag, he was a 32-year-old former
smoke jumper and union leader Montana, who ran on lowering costs, giving working people a stronger
voice in Washington. His victory gives Democrats their first house seat from Montana in more than
30 years. There's candidate like Rebecca Cook, 38-year-old former waitress, small business
owner, nonprofit founder in Wisconsin. She flipped a house seat in a largely rural district by being
Republican incumbent and MAGA die-hard Derek Van Orten. Senator Bernie Sanders, independent of
Vermont, traveled the country campaigning for candidates like Rebecca Cook and Sam Forstag.
Senator Sanders says the candidates he endorsed won 15 of 16 house races,
three out of four Senate seats and flipped six Republican-held house seats, and Senator Sanders
joins me now. Senator, you're a man who has been through a lot of election nights in your life,
quite a few. And you've been personally and with your, you know, people that you believe in on
the right side and the wrong side of some of those, depending on the night, where does Tuesday
night rank in a lifetime's worth of election night? Well, Chris, let me say this. I feel,
I hell of a lot better tonight than I did a couple of days ago. It was an extraordinary victory.
And now with a strong Democratic majority in the House, good majority in the Senate,
our job is to stand up for working families, take on the oligarchy and restore faith in American
democracy. We've got to deliver for working families. That's what we've got to do.
I looked at some of the candidates that you endorsed and campaigned with. Some of them,
I think, like Abdul Assyed, I think you would call progressive and recognizably so.
But Sam Forstag and Rebecca Cook in these districts that are swingier. You know,
it's reminded of your own politics in Vermont where you were never a big person on limiting,
like, gun ownership. And I remember an interview you gave with Vox back in 2016,
where you talked about your opposition to what you called open borders and that
being a chamber of commerce issue. You were very opposed to defunding the police,
even when it was a slogan that had some real credence in Democratic parties. Are there things
you have to do to be a kind of populist Democrat in places that do have some conservatism in them
and still win? Look, Chris, every district and every part of the country are different.
Every candidate is different. But here is the bottom line. Whether you're in Wisconsin,
whether you're in Mississippi, whether you're in Vermont, you understand that there is something
wrong when in the richest country in the history of the world, tens of millions of Americans
are struggling to put food on the table, pay for healthcare, pay for housing,
while the very richest people have never, ever had it so good. And I think that common theme
that it is time that we stood up to the billionaire class and delivered for working
families, that is what our candidates talked about. That's why they won.
That 15 seconds from you, which I have heard from you many times, and the many times that
we have spoken, is one that clearly can travel. Because, you know, that's not that different
than what James Tallarico was saying in Texas and the state he carried by 12 or what I'll do
outside or what Troy Jackson said in Maine. Like that was that, that, that when you said
right there, I think it was pretty common. Now the question of what, what do you do about that
with power when you don't have the White House? All right. That's the question, Chris. You got it.
Okay. All right. A lot of people are good on rhetoric. Let's get to the facts. The United
States today is spending twice as much per capita on healthcare as the people, any other country,
and yet we're the only major country on earth not to guarantee healthcare to all people.
That absurdity has got to end. Healthcare is a human right. We need Medicare for all,
which is now supported by over 60% of Americans, probably 80, 90% of Democrats. Number two,
we have more income than wealth. Can I stop you there, though, because
let me just stop you there, because I'm on a roll, Chris. I was going to go through 10 points,
but all right. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. But let me just stop you there, because I mean, obviously,
I know you believe this. I looked at the polling. It's very clear polling on Medicare for all has
gone up. It was very interesting that Abdul El Sayed was attacked for a million things in that,
in that race, but not for that. But I think you and I would agree the odds of Donald Trump signing
that into law, pretty small. So you're going to have two House majorities. You're going to have
a Senate and a House, right? Hold it. Hold it. Hold it. Hold it. Two points. Okay.
Point number one, Trump has the constitutional right to do to veto. He wants to do it.
But we have the constitutional right to represent the American people and to pass the damn thing
and to show the American people that we are sick and tired of maintaining a broken system.
Number two, you know what? Donald Trump may be a bit crazy, but he is not stupid.
And he is a good politician. This guy looks out all over the country and he says,
oh my God, everybody knows the system is broken. You know what? What do I got to lose?
So I am not absolutely certain that Trump would not sign it. But whether he would or not,
our job is to produce it. He wants to veto it. Republicans want to sustain that veto.
That is their responsibility. The American people will see it.
Number two, an issue that we don't talk about enough, I do.
We have more income and wealth inequality today than ever before in American history.
The American people want a tax on billionaires so that we can have universal child care,
we can make public colleges free, tuition free, and we can build millions of units
of low income and affordable housing. In other words, we can't just talk about affordability.
You've got to have the guts to take on the big money people. It's time that the billionaire class,
many of whom pay an effective tax rate lower than a truck driver,
start paying their fair share of taxes. Thirdly, we have got to end this endless war.
I'll cut it short for you. Do your favor. Cut it short. We have to end endless wars,
no more financial support for the extremist government of Israel.
On the endless wars, and let me put those into two categories. On Iran specifically,
it seems to me that votes to stop the war, to stop, to not fund it, to even maybe play
hardball on funding the government unless there's a negotiated settlement to the war,
it does strike me that that's a thing that I think you could probably get
every member of the incoming caucus on. I mean, really, I think almost without exception,
you could probably get the 55, 56, or 54 senators and the 250 plus members of the House.
Is that your sense, too? Absolutely. And there will be some Republicans on board as well.
It's not only Vance who understands this war is a disaster, a lot of Republicans do.
But again, our job is to be bold, to be bold. Trump wants to veto stuff, it's his privilege.
We have got to distinguish ourselves from the Republicans.
All right, Senator Bernie Sanders, thanks for your time, and I appreciate it.
Okay, thank you. All right, we'll talk again soon. We'll be right back.
